lessons.title: Greetings
lessons.notes: Ciao is informal and means both hello and goodbye. Buongiorno and buonasera are polite greetings.

lessons.title: Asking for help
lessons.notes: Come si dice…? asks how to say a word or phrase. Puoi is informal singular; può is the polite singular form.

lessons.title: Being polite
lessons.notes: Buona serata wishes someone a pleasant evening when parting. Buonasera is a greeting. Per favore makes a request polite.

lessons.title: Everyday essentials
lessons.notes: Italian often omits subject pronouns: hai already means you have. Dov’è combines dove + è. Devo is followed by an infinitive: devo andare.

lessons.title: Numbers 1–20
lessons.notes: Memorize 1–20 as the building blocks. The number sei (six) is spelled like tu sei (you are); context tells you the meaning.

lessons.title: Numbers 21–100
lessons.notes: Write tens + units as one word. Drop the final vowel of the tens before uno or otto: ventuno, ventotto. Compounds ending in tre take an acute accent: ventitré, quarantatré; tre alone has none.

lessons.title: Days, dates & telling time

cards.no: hvilken dag er det i dag?

cards.en: it is the first of May
it is the second of May

cards.it: sono le otto e un quarto
sono le nove meno un quarto

lessons.notes: Days and months normally use lowercase. Use primo for the first day of a month and cardinal numbers after that. For clock time use è l’una, è mezzogiorno, è mezzanotte, but sono le… for other hours. E mezza means half past; meno un quarto means quarter to. Alle introduces a time, but use all’una. Clock examples come from PDF p. 26.

lessons.title: Months & seasons
lessons.notes: Months and seasons normally have lowercase initials in Italian. In primavera / estate / autunno / inverno means in spring / summer / autumn / winter.

lessons.title: Alphabet & pronunciation

cards.en: c sounds like ch in chip
cards.no: c uttales som tsj i tsjekkisk

cards.en: ch sounds like k in key
g sounds like j in gin
gh sounds like g in give
gn is a single ny-like sound
gli usually has a palatal l sound
cards.no: gli har vanligvis en lj-lignende lyd

cards.en: qu sounds like kw in queen
cards.no: qu uttales som k etterfulgt av engelsk w

cards.en: sc before e or i sounds like sh
cards.no: sc foran e eller i har en sj-lyd

cards.en: c before a, o or u has a hard k sound
cards.no: c foran a, o eller u har en hard k-lyd

cards.en: g before a, o or u has a hard g sound
cards.no: g foran a, o eller u har en hard g-lyd

lessons.notes: Sound guides are approximations, not English spellings. C and g are soft before e/i; h keeps them hard in che/chi and ghe/ghi. Gli has the palatal sound in figlio and famiglia, but not in every word: glicine has hard gl. Double consonants are held longer. Stress usually falls on the next-to-last syllable, with exceptions.
lessons.alphabet: A a · B bi · C ci · D di · E e · F effe · G gi · H acca · I i · L elle · M emme · N enne · O o · P pi · Q cu · R erre · S esse · T ti · U u · V vu (also vi) · Z zeta. Letters in loanwords: J i lunga · K cappa · W doppia vu · X ics · Y ipsilon.

lessons.title: Noun gender
lessons.notes: Nouns have grammatical gender. Most nouns in -o are masculine and most in -a feminine, but there are exceptions. Nouns in -e can be either: il fiore, la notte. Learn each noun with its article.

lessons.title: Plural -o → -i
lessons.notes: Most nouns ending in -o change to -i in the plural. This is a pattern, not a rule for every noun. Masculine plural can also refer to a mixed group.

lessons.title: Plural -a → -e
lessons.notes: Most feminine nouns ending in -a change to -e. This does not apply to masculine nouns such as il problema → i problemi. Preserve a hard c/g before e with h when needed: amica → amiche.

lessons.title: Plural -e → -i
lessons.notes: Nouns ending in -e usually change to -i, whether masculine or feminine. The ending alone does not reveal gender: il fiore, la notte.

lessons.title: Definite articles
lessons.notes: Masculine: il → i before most consonants; l’ → gli before vowels. Feminine: la or l’ → le. Elision in l’amica does not change its gender; its plural is le amiche.

lessons.title: Special & indefinite articles
lessons.notes: Masculine lo/uno precede s + consonant, z, gn, ps, pn, x and consonantal y; lo becomes gli in the plural. Use un before other masculine nouns, including vowels: un amico (no apostrophe). Feminine una becomes un’ before a vowel: un’amica. Borrowed nouns are often unchanged in the plural, but are not always masculine.

lessons.title: Subject pronouns
lessons.notes: The six verb persons are io, tu, lui/lei, noi, voi, loro. Italian commonly omits subject pronouns. Formal Lei means you and takes the third-person singular verb form; voi is plural.

lessons.title: Regular -are
lessons.notes: Remove -are and add -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano. These models are from PDF p. 11. Some verbs need spelling changes; do not apply the pattern blindly to irregular verbs.

lessons.title: Regular -ere
lessons.notes: Remove -ere and add -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ete, -ono. Scrivere and vedere follow this pattern in the present tense.

lessons.title: Regular -ire
lessons.notes: Dormire and aprire use -o, -i, -e, -iamo, -ite, -ono. Supplement: some -ire verbs insert -isc- in io/tu/lui-lei/loro, e.g. capire: capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono. The dormire pattern does not cover all -ire verbs.

lessons.title: Essere & avere
lessons.notes: Essere and avere are irregular. Sono can mean I am or they are; pronouns make the cards unambiguous. The h in ho, hai, ha, hanno is silent. Use avere for age and hunger: ho venti anni, ho fame.

lessons.title: Andare & venire
lessons.notes: Andare means to go, whether walking or using transport. Venire means to come toward the speaker or another relevant person/place; venire da can express origin. All six present-tense forms are shown for each verb.

lessons.title: Fare — doing & making

conjugations.meaning: to do / make · å gjøre / lage

lessons.notes: Fare means to do or make and is irregular. Fa has no accent in the present tense. Learn fixed expressions such as fare colazione as whole phrases.

lessons.title: Question words I
lessons.notes: A question mark and intonation can turn a statement into a question without changing word order. Perché means why in a question and because in an answer; spell it with an acute accent.

lessons.title: Question words II
lessons.notes: Quale → quali agrees in number. Quanto changes with gender and number before a noun: quanto, quanta, quanti, quante. Use quante sigarette, not quanti sigarette.

lessons.title: Negation
lessons.notes: Put non before the verb. When mai, niente or nessuno follows the verb, non is normally also needed: non mangio mai; non vedo niente. This is normal Italian, not an error. Nessuno before the verb needs no non: nessuno parla.

lessons.title: Question practice
lessons.notes: Italian does not need English do/does to make a question. In quanto costa?, costa is third-person singular. Use costano for plural things.

lessons.title: Adjective gender
lessons.notes: An adjective agrees with the noun’s gender and number. Basic -o adjectives have -o/-a/-i/-e forms. Bello and buono can change form before a noun; these cards teach their basic forms.

lessons.title: Adjective plurals
lessons.notes: Use -i for masculine plural and -e for feminine plural with these -o adjectives. Agreement follows gender and number, not simply the noun’s final vowel.

lessons.title: Adjectives in -e
lessons.notes: Adjectives in -e have one singular form for both genders and a plural in -i: un ragazzo gentile, una ragazza gentile, persone gentili.

lessons.title: Describing people
lessons.notes: Keep subject and verb in agreement: il ragazzo è, i ragazzi sono. Gentile works for both singular genders; bello changes to bella.

lessons.title: Adjective review
lessons.notes: Bravo/brava commonly means good at something or capable, not simply intelligent. Many colour adjectives agree (rosso/rossa/rossi/rosse); blu, rosa, viola and lilla are invariable. See PDF p. 22.

lessons.title: Volere — want

conjugations.meaning: to want · å ville / ville ha

lessons.notes: Volere + infinitive means to want to do something: voglio parlare. Volere + noun means to want something: voglio il gelato (jeg vil ha iskrem).

lessons.title: Potere — can
lessons.notes: Potere + infinitive expresses permission, possibility or ability in the circumstances. For a learned skill, use sapere + infinitive. Può has an accent.

lessons.title: Dovere — must
lessons.notes: Dovere + infinitive means must or have to. The following infinitive stays unchanged: dobbiamo studiare. Devo and devono also have the variants debbo and debbono.

lessons.title: Sapere — know how

conjugations.meaning: to know / know how · å vite / kunne

lessons.notes: Sapere can mean to know information (so la risposta) or know how to do something (so nuotare). Norwegian often uses vet for information and kan for a learned skill. Use an infinitive after sapere for a skill.

lessons.title: Modals in sentences

cards.en: I know how to speak Italian

lessons.notes: Conjugate the modal, leaving the following verb in the infinitive: voglio parlare, puoi ripetere, devo studiare, so parlare. Do not conjugate both verbs.

lessons.title: A short message
lessons.notes: These phrases are adapted from the message on PDF p. 30. Non posso gives inability, devo lavorare gives the reason, and puoi andare? asks for help.

lessons.title: Fare in daily life
lessons.notes: Fare appears in fixed expressions. Fare colazione means eat breakfast, whereas preparare la colazione means prepare breakfast. Fare la spesa means grocery shopping.

lessons.title: Weather with fare
lessons.notes: Weather expressions use impersonal third-person singular fa: fa caldo, fa freddo. To say you feel hot or cold, use ho caldo / ho freddo.

lessons.title: Speaking review
lessons.notes: Review complete phrases aloud. Devo andare can mean I must go or I have to go. Quanto costa? asks how much it costs.

lessons.title: Grammar review
lessons.notes: Check articles, noun number and verb person together: il libro → i libri, la casa → le case. Io sono means I am, while loro sono means they are.

lessons.title: Final A1 review
lessons.notes: Review agreement, negation and modal + infinitive patterns. Repeat missed cards; a quiz score checks these study items and is not an official A1 proficiency assessment.
